To establish a rigorous baseline, we first align Sigma ’s data, architecture, and optimization with discrete dLMs for a controlled comparison at scale ( Sec. 3.2.1 ). In Sec. 3.2.2 , we evaluate the impact of AR initialization when pre-training Sigma -3B with 3 , followed by an investigation of AR regularization for training our flagship 3B/8B models. Proper AR initialization/regularization leads to the best Sigma model. 3.2.1 Unified Pre-training of Continuous and Discrete dLMs Data. As with NLD, we adopt the open-sourced pre-training data from Basant et al. (2025) . We use the Mistral-NeMo tokenizer ( V = 131,072 V=131{,}072 ) ( Mistral AI, 2024 ) , batch size 512 512 , and L = 4096 L=4096 . Architecture. Sigma adopts the transformer backbone of NLD and its AR baseline, ensuring the three families are parameter- and FLOP-matched. As with NLD, Sigma uses a block causal attention mask ( Fig. 2(b) ). Sigma uniquely adds a unit-norm 16-dimensional diffusion embedding table with a linear up-projection, a categorical reparameterization mapping V V -dimensional probabilities to low-dimensional soft embeddings, a self-conditioning linear projection, Fourier time conditioning, and a learnable noise schedule (see Sec. 2 ). Together, these account for less than 1 % 1\% of the total parameters. We provide thorough details in App. E . Training. We train our models for 150K steps, following the optimization procedure detailed in App. E . Given a batch size of 512, 150K steps correspond to over 300B tokens. Training consumed ~9,600 and ~19,200 NVIDIA GB200 GPU hours for the 3B and 8B models, respectively. 3.2.2 AR Initialization and Regularization AR Initialization. To evaluate the impact of initialization, we compare pre-training Sigma ( i ) from scratch and ( ii ) from an AR baseline pretrained on 1T tokens. Due to the dimension mismatch between high-dimensional AR embeddings and Sigma ’s 16-dimensional space, we randomly initialize the diffusion embedding layer. As shown in Figs. 3(a) and 3(b) , Sigma -3B ( L ′ = 64 L^{\prime}{=}64 ) with self-conditioning achieves competitive perplexity relative to NLD-3B ( L ′ = 64 L^{\prime}{=}64 ) under both regimes (i) and (ii). However, AR initialization significantly accelerates convergence and yields lower final training loss. AR Regularization. Continuous diffusion training inherently suffers from high gradient variance and slow convergence. To mitigate variance and accelerate optimization, we follow NLD by adding AR regularization, optimizing the joint objective ℒ ar + w diff ​ ℒ BD \mathcal{L}_{\text{ar}}+w_{\text{diff}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{BD}} ( Fig. 3(c) ; see App. E for the w diff w_{\text{diff}} weighting schedule), where ℒ ar = ∑ l = 2 L − log ⟨ 𝐱 θ l ( 𝐱 < l ) , 𝐱 l ⟩ \mathcal{L}_{\text{ar}}={\textstyle\sum}_{l=2}^{L}-\log\langle{\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}^{l}({\mathbf{x}}^{<l}),{\mathbf{x}}^{l}\rangle (6) is computed over the AR stream using causal attention ( Fig. 2 ). This architecture employs two distinct readout heads, with the AR regularization computed exclusively from the AR head. While this dual-head formulation improves auxiliary AR decoding capability, our primary objective remains maximizing diffusion decoding performance. Finally, input sequences utilize AR embeddings for the AR stream and 16D diffusion embeddings for the diffusion stream ( Fig. 2 ), facilitating AR initialization and efficient KV-caching. As shown in Fig. 3(c) , AR regularization significantly improves training stability; with a properly tuned w diff w_{\text{diff}} , it even outperforms pure perplexity optimization for the diffusion stream. This confirms that AR regularization stabilizes training while yielding a higher-quality model. Classifier-free guidance (CFG). CFG ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) is the standard tool for class-conditional or text-to-image diffusion models. In CFG, one queries the model twice to obtain a conditional and an unconditional prediction and then linearly extrapolates them. For our block diffusion model, the clean context 𝐜 {\mathbf{c}} serves as the natural conditioning information, and CFG extrapolates away from the unconditional prediction for the current block b {\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b} : 𝐞 θ w ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) , t , 𝐜 ) := 𝐞 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) , t , ∅ ) + w ⁡ [ 𝐞 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) , t , 𝐜 ) − 𝐞 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t ( b ) , t , ∅ ) ] , \displaystyle{\mathbf{e}}^{w}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}}):={\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;\varnothing)+w\,\big[{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}})-{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;\varnothing)\big], (CFG) where ∅ \varnothing drops the entire clean context 𝐜 {\mathbf{c}} (so 𝐳 t ( b ) {\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})} attends only within its own block) and w ≥ 1 w\geq 1 is the guidance strength ( w = 1 w=1 falls back to the plain conditional prediction). First, at batch size 1 1 transformer inference is memory-bound, so we pack conditional and unconditional predictions into a single forward pass at almost no wall-clock cost ( Liu et al., 2026b ) , using the packed mask of Fig. 4(a) .
